name: Light box (SAD lamp)

card.summary: A bright-light lamp used for seasonal depression, with solid evidence for SAD and none yet for looks.
card.aka: SAD lamp, bright light therapy box, light therapy lamp, happy light
card.note: Evidence supports mood effects in seasonal affective disorder; appearance benefits are untested. People with mania tendency or eye or skin photosensitivity are advised to seek clinical advice.

quick.overview:
A light box, or SAD lamp, is a bright lamp that emits up to about 10,000 lux of filtered white light, far above ordinary indoor lighting. It is sitting-in-front-of-it therapy, usually used in the morning for seasonal affective disorder, a pattern of winter depression.

In looksmaxxing and fitness circles it comes up as a way to improve energy, mood, sleep timing and winter low spirits that people link to how they look and perform. A 2020 meta-analysis found bright light superior to placebo for SAD, but no study has tested light boxes for facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Bright light is detected by light-sensitive retinal cells that suppress melatonin and help reset the body clock. Researchers also link seasonal depression to serotonin function and to a phase-delay of circadian rhythms, which morning light is thought to advance.
quick.risks: Reported side effects include headache, eye irritation, jumpiness and nausea, and light therapy can trigger mania in people prone to it. Sources list eye conditions sensitive to light, photosensitive skin conditions, porphyria and photosensitizing drugs or herbs as reasons for caution, and recommend clinician supervision.

lead: A light box, commonly called a SAD lamp, is a device that gives off bright white light, typically up to 10,000 lux at a set distance, used for bright light therapy (BLT).[1][2] It is the standard form of light therapy for seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a condition of recurrent winter depression that affects about 1 to 3 percent of adults in temperate climates and is more common in women.[3][4]

A 2020 meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials found that bright light therapy of at least 1,000 lux was superior to dim-light or sham placebo for depression ratings and for treatment response in SAD, although the authors noted moderate heterogeneity and a moderate-to-high risk of bias.[1] Light therapy has also been studied in non-seasonal depression, sleep problems in older adults, and agitation in dementia.[5][6][7]

In appearance-focused communities, light boxes are occasionally mentioned as a mood or energy tool, and some users note that lamps sold online are weaker than clinic-grade units.[8] No clinical studies have tested light boxes for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Up to about 10,000 lux at a set distance; 2,000 to 10,000 lux for 30 to 120 minutes daily in classic protocols[2][3]
Modern SAD lamps filter or do not emit UV[2]

paras: A light box contains fluorescent or LED lamps behind a diffusing screen. Classic SAD treatment has the user sit in front of the box for roughly 30 to 120 minutes a day during the winter at 2,000 to 10,000 lux.[3] Some devices use lower-intensity blue (about 460 nm) or green (about 525 nm) light instead of white, and a 1995 study reported that green light at 350 lux produced melatonin suppression and phase shifts comparable to 10,000 lux white light.[2]

Modern lamps made for SAD and sleep disorders either filter out or do not emit ultraviolet light.[2] Other light-therapy forms include light visors and dawn simulators, which Wikipedia says have similar success rates to bright light.[2]

Heliotherapy appears in ancient medical traditions, and Niels Finsen developed early artificial phototherapy and won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[2] Light therapy was mainstream in the UK from the late 1800s to the early 1930s, and Dora Colebrook's controlled trials later found it ineffective for many of the conditions it had been used for.[2]
Bright light treatment of seasonal depression has been in clinical use for over 30 years.[1]

Light suppresses melatonin production and resets the body's internal clock via photosensitive ganglion cells in the retina.[2] The phase-delay hypothesis holds that SAD patients' circadian rhythms are delayed relative to their sleep-wake cycle, so that phase-advancing light, typically in the morning, should help; serotonin dysfunction has also been implicated.[3] Morning treatment has given the best results.[2]

For SAD, the 2020 meta-analysis reported a standardised mean difference of -0.37 for depression ratings (18 studies, 610 patients) and a risk ratio of 1.42 for response (16 studies, 559 patients) against placebo.[1] The review concluded that bright light therapy can be regarded as an effective SAD treatment, with evidence from methodologically heterogeneous studies.[1]

For non-seasonal depression, Wikipedia summarises Cochrane and later meta-analyses as showing modest benefit, with a 2015 review finding the evidence limited by methodological flaws.[2] A Cochrane review has examined bright light for sleep problems in adults aged 60 and over.[9]

The Can-SAD trial compared light therapy with fluoxetine in winter seasonal affective disorder, and a 2016 JAMA Psychiatry randomized trial tested light, fluoxetine and their combination against sham in non-seasonal major depression.[10][5] A pilot randomized trial in Macao with 31 older adults with dementia reported significant reductions in agitation in outdoor and indoor light-box groups over four weeks versus controls, with no difference in cognition between groups.[7]
No studies found examining light boxes for skin, facial appearance or other cosmetic outcomes.

Wikipedia lists side effects in some conditions as jumpiness, headache, eye irritation and nausea, and says light therapy can trigger mania or anxiety.[2] Contraindications named there include eye conditions that increase vulnerability to phototoxicity, a tendency toward mania, photosensitive skin conditions, photosensitizing herbs or drugs such as St. John's wort, and porphyria.[2] The same source recommends supervision by an experienced clinician.[2]
A review of mood-disorder management in pregnancy notes that light box therapy has some support for treating depressive episodes but lacks evidence for preventing relapse.[11]

On T Nation, a poster who said a clinician had prescribed light therapy wrote that lamps sold on Amazon are 'severely underpowered' and work only at about 5 to 6 inches from the face for 30 minutes or more daily.[8] Another poster said he might get a SAD light because he felt sleepy in winter.[12]

timeline.event: Niels Finsen receives the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on phototherapy.[2]
A study reports green light at 350 lux produces melatonin suppression and phase shifts comparable to 10,000 lux white light.[2]

lore.intro: Light boxes are not a core looksmaxxing topic, but they appear in fitness-forum talk about winter mood, sleep and energy.[8][12]

claims.claim: Consumer SAD lamps are too weak to work unless held very close
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says Amazon lamps are 'severely underpowered' and 'technically' work only at 5 to 6 inches for 30+ minutes.[8]
claims.experts: Clinical protocols describe 2,000 to 10,000 lux for 30 to 120 minutes daily, and trials use at least 1,000 lux.[1][3] No study reviewed compared consumer and clinical devices.

claims.claim: A light lamp can fix winter tiredness and low mood
claims.believers: A poster who felt like 'sleeping all the time' in winter wondered about a SAD light.[12]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis found bright light superior to placebo in diagnosed SAD with a small to moderate effect size.[1]
